name: Communication & Media
tagline: From messages and stories to journalism, platforms and communication research.

nodes.title: Messages, Pictures and Listening
nodes.goal: Recognize that words, pictures and sounds can carry a message.
learning_outcomes: Recognize speech, images and gestures as messages.
Identify a message sender and receiver.
Ask or show when a meaning is unclear.

lesson.overview: A message is something one person communicates to another. We can use speech, gestures, pictures and sounds. A picture of a cup may show where cups belong; a bell may tell a group that an activity is changing. The receiver needs to understand the sign, so a message can be unclear if people use different meanings. Listening and asking can help us check what someone meant.
lesson.worked_example: A child points to a picture of a drink. An adult checks, “Would you like water?” The picture helps communicate a need, and the question checks its meaning.
lesson.activity: Make a picture sign for a toy box. Ask a partner what it means, then change it if the meaning is unclear.
lesson.reflection: How can you show an idea without speaking?

quiz.prompt: A picture on a toy box can tell us?
quiz.explain: A picture sign can communicate where things belong.
quiz.say: A picture on a toy box can tell us?

quiz.prompt: Can pointing be a message?
quiz.explain: Gestures can carry meaning.
quiz.say: Can pointing be a message?

quiz.prompt: You do not understand a sign. What helps?
quiz.explain: Asking checks the intended meaning.
quiz.say: You do not understand a sign. What helps?

quiz.prompt: When a friend speaks, listening helps you?
quiz.explain: Listening gives attention to what the person communicates.
quiz.say: When a friend speaks, listening helps you?

quiz.prompt: A bell means tidy-up time in your class. What carries the message?
quiz.explain: Sounds can signal shared meanings.
quiz.say: A bell means tidy-up time in your class. What carries the message?

quiz.prompt: Your friend misunderstands your picture. What can you do?
quiz.explain: A clearer representation can help the receiver understand.
quiz.say: Your friend misunderstands your picture. What can you do?

nodes.kid_text: Words, pictures, sounds and pointing can all share a message. Listen and look. If you are unsure, ask what the message means.

nodes.title: Pretend Stories and Real Events
nodes.goal: Distinguish make-believe from reports about real events with adult support.
learning_outcomes: Identify an obvious make-believe feature.
Describe what a picture actually shows.
Seek support to check a confusing message.

lesson.overview: Stories can be invented for fun, or they can tell us about something that happened. A talking moon in a picture book is make-believe, while a photograph of a family walk records light from a scene. Pictures alone do not always tell the whole story: people can draw, stage or change them. Young learners do not need to solve every puzzle alone; a trusted adult can help check a surprising or upsetting message.
lesson.worked_example: A cartoon cat flies to the moon with a balloon. The family laughs at the imagined adventure. Later, a real photograph shows a cat sitting by a window; they describe only what the picture actually shows.
lesson.activity: With an adult, compare one pretend story and one account of your day. Name a clue about each and ask a question about anything uncertain.
lesson.reflection: Can a pretend story be enjoyable even when it did not happen?

quiz.prompt: A dragon in a story talks. This is usually?
quiz.explain: Invented stories can include impossible events.
quiz.say: A dragon in a story talks. This is usually?

quiz.prompt: Can we enjoy a story that did not happen?
quiz.explain: Fiction can entertain and help us imagine.
quiz.say: Can we enjoy a story that did not happen?

quiz.prompt: A picture shows a dog beside a bowl. What can you safely say?
choices: The dog is beside a bowl
quiz.answer: The dog is beside a bowl
quiz.explain: Describe visible evidence without adding unsupported details.
quiz.say: A picture shows a dog beside a bowl. What can you safely say?

quiz.prompt: A video scares or confuses you. What helps?
quiz.explain: An adult can help explain and check what you saw.
quiz.say: A video scares or confuses you. What helps?

quiz.prompt: Can someone draw an imaginary place?
quiz.explain: Drawings can show invented scenes.
quiz.say: Can someone draw an imaginary place?

quiz.prompt: A friend says a surprising thing happened. What can you do?
quiz.explain: Asking about evidence helps distinguish a report from imagination.
quiz.say: A friend says a surprising thing happened. What can you do?

nodes.kid_text: Some stories are pretend. Some tell us about real events. Pictures can leave things out or be changed. Ask a trusted grown-up when a message is confusing.

nodes.title: Who Made This Message?
nodes.goal: Identify the source, audience and purpose of a simple message.
learning_outcomes: Identify a message source.
Distinguish informing, entertaining and persuading.
Explain why appearance is not evidence of accuracy.

lesson.overview: Messages are made by people or organizations for an audience. A notice may inform, a story may entertain, and an advertisement may encourage someone to buy or choose something. A single message can have several purposes. Asking who made it, who it is for and what it asks us to do gives us a useful starting point. A colourful or friendly design does not tell us whether a claim is accurate.
lesson.worked_example: A poster says a toy is “the best ever” and shows children smiling. It is made by the toy seller for possible buyers. The pictures may attract attention, but they do not prove the toy is best for every child.
lesson.activity: Compare a school notice, a story cover and a pretend advertisement. Name the maker, audience and likely purpose of each.
lesson.reflection: What might a message leave out when its maker wants you to buy something?

quiz.prompt: A poster from a toy seller asks you to buy. Its main purpose is?
quiz.explain: Advertisements often aim to influence choices.
quiz.say: A poster from a toy seller asks you to buy. Its main purpose is?

quiz.prompt: The audience is?
choices: The people a message is intended for
quiz.answer: The people a message is intended for
quiz.explain: Audience names the intended receivers.
quiz.say: The audience is?

quiz.prompt: A school notice gives the library opening time. It mainly?
quiz.explain: The notice provides practical information.
quiz.say: A school notice gives the library opening time. It mainly?

quiz.prompt: A bright design proves a claim is true?
quiz.explain: Appearance and accuracy are different.
quiz.say: A bright design proves a claim is true?

quiz.prompt: What question helps identify a source?
quiz.explain: Knowing the maker provides context for evaluating a message.
quiz.say: What question helps identify a source?

quiz.prompt: Can a message both entertain and persuade?
quiz.explain: Purposes can overlap in one message.
quiz.say: Can a message both entertain and persuade?

nodes.kid_text: Ask who made a message and who it is for. Is it telling you something, making you laugh, or asking you to choose or buy? A pretty picture is not proof.

nodes.title: Create a Clear and Respectful Message
nodes.goal: Plan a short message that matches its audience and respects privacy.
learning_outcomes: Match a message to an audience and purpose.
Include essential practical details.
Use consent and privacy checks before sharing.

lesson.overview: A clear message has a purpose and includes the details its audience needs. Words and pictures should work together: a notice about a puppet show needs the time and place, while decoration should not hide them. Sharing also creates responsibilities. We ask before including another person’s picture, avoid revealing private information, and make sure a trusted adult approves public sharing. A draft can be improved by asking someone what they understood.
lesson.worked_example: A class designs a pretend invitation to a puppet show. The first draft has a large puppet but no time. A partner’s question reveals the missing detail, so the class adds it and uses drawings instead of unapproved photographs of children.
lesson.activity: Make a pretend event notice using an invented place and time. Test it with a partner, add missing information, and check that it contains no real private details.
lesson.reflection: What did your audience need that you initially forgot?

quiz.prompt: A notice for a show needs?
choices: A secret password to your home
quiz.explain: Practical details help the audience act on the message.
quiz.say: A notice for a show needs?

quiz.prompt: Before using a friend’s photo, you should?
choices: Ask permission and get adult guidance
quiz.answer: Ask permission and get adult guidance
quiz.explain: People should have a choice about sharing their image.
quiz.say: Before using a friend’s photo, you should?

quiz.prompt: Which detail should stay out of a public class poster?
quiz.explain: Home addresses are private information.
quiz.say: Which detail should stay out of a public class poster?

quiz.prompt: A partner cannot read the tiny text. What can improve the notice?
choices: Make important text clear and larger
quiz.answer: Make important text clear and larger
quiz.explain: Readability supports the audience’s needs.
quiz.say: A partner cannot read the tiny text. What can improve the notice?

quiz.prompt: Testing a draft with a reader helps you?
quiz.explain: Audience feedback reveals communication gaps.
quiz.say: Testing a draft with a reader helps you?

quiz.prompt: For practice, the safest event details are?
choices: Invented details checked by an adult
quiz.answer: Invented details checked by an adult
quiz.explain: Fictional practice details avoid exposing personal information.
quiz.say: For practice, the safest event details are?

nodes.kid_text: Make your message clear. Include what people need to know. Ask before sharing someone’s picture, keep private details private, and let a trusted grown-up help.

nodes.title: Checking Claims and Sources
nodes.goal: Trace a claim to evidence and compare genuinely independent sources.
learning_outcomes: State a checkable claim precisely.
Trace an assertion to its original evidence.
Distinguish repetition from independent corroboration.

lesson.overview: Verification begins with a precise claim: what exactly is being asserted, about where and when? The next step is to trace its source and inspect the evidence behind it. Many websites can repeat one original report, so repetition is not the same as independent confirmation. Dates, context and the method used to produce a number matter. A responsible check can conclude that a claim is supported, contradicted or still uncertain, and the conclusion should match the strength of the evidence.
lesson.worked_example: Three posts say a local pond has dried up, but all copy one old article from another town. A date check and the original article show the posts do not establish what happened to the local pond today.
lesson.activity: Use a fictional packet of posts, an original report and a data table. Write the exact claim, trace dependencies between sources, and give a verdict with one remaining uncertainty.
lesson.reflection: When should you say “I do not have enough evidence” rather than forcing a true-or-false verdict?

quiz.prompt: Five sites copy one report. How many independent reports is that?
quiz.explain: Copies share the same evidential origin.

quiz.prompt: A claim says “the lake is empty.” What context is missing?
choices: The colour of the page border
quiz.explain: Place and time determine what must be checked.

quiz.prompt: An old accurate photo is presented as today’s event. The problem is?
quiz.explain: Authentic material can be misrepresented by false timing.

quiz.prompt: The best next step after finding a statistic is often?
quiz.explain: Provenance and methods help establish what the number means.

quiz.prompt: Two independent witnesses agree. This provides?
quiz.explain: Independent agreement can strengthen evidence but remains fallible.

quiz.prompt: Evidence is incomplete. A responsible verdict is?
choices: The claim is established as false
The claim is established as true
quiz.explain: Uncertainty is appropriate when support is insufficient.

quiz.prompt: Which source detail matters for a survey claim?
choices: The size of the publisher’s logo
The name of the downloaded file
quiz.explain: Sampling affects what population the result represents.

quiz.prompt: A headline makes a stronger claim than its article. Check?
quiz.explain: Headlines can overstate the body or evidence.

quiz.prompt: A correction appears after publication. You should?
choices: Treat correction as proof of fraud
Give priority to the first version
quiz.explain: Corrections can improve accuracy and should be evaluated.

quiz.prompt: A source is usually reliable. Does every new claim become certain?
quiz.explain: Reputation is useful context, not a guarantee.

quiz.prompt: Four posts repeat an old report from a different town to describe today’s local event. Explain a responsible verification response.
quiz.answer: Trace the posts to their original source and check the date and location. Repetition is not independent evidence, so the current local claim remains uncertain without relevant corroboration.
quiz.explain: Trace the posts to their original source and check the date and location. Repetition is not independent evidence, so the current local claim remains uncertain without relevant corroboration.

nodes.title: Images, Framing and Visual Stories
nodes.goal: Explain how selection, sequence and captions shape an image-based message.
learning_outcomes: Describe the effect of framing and cropping.
Write a context-preserving caption.
Distinguish documentary images from illustrations.

lesson.overview: A photograph records a selected view at a selected moment. Framing determines what appears inside the image and what remains outside it. Cropping, captions and sequence can change interpretation without changing the visible objects themselves. Illustration can explain an idea that a photograph cannot show directly, but readers should know whether an image is a record, a reconstruction or an imagined scene. Ethical visual storytelling preserves relevant context and avoids presenting fabricated details as documentary evidence.
lesson.worked_example: A close crop shows three people in a crowded corner, while a wider frame reveals an almost empty hall. Captioning the crop “the whole hall was packed” overstates what the view supports.
lesson.activity: Create two paper frames over the same classroom drawing. Describe how each selection changes the story, then write a caption that states only supported context.
lesson.reflection: What information outside a picture could change its meaning?

quiz.prompt: Cropping an image changes?
quiz.explain: Selection can alter interpretation without changing the event.

quiz.prompt: A close-up of three people proves an entire hall was full?
choices: No, the frame omits the rest
quiz.answer: No, the frame omits the rest
quiz.explain: The frame does not show the whole hall.

quiz.prompt: A useful caption supplies?
quiz.explain: Context helps readers interpret the image accurately.

quiz.prompt: An illustration of an imagined future should be labelled?
choices: A photograph of a documented event
Direct evidence of a past occurrence
quiz.explain: The label distinguishes explanation or imagination from documentation.

quiz.prompt: Two images in sequence can imply?
quiz.explain: Juxtaposition can suggest connections not established by evidence.

quiz.prompt: A dramatic camera angle is evidence of?
quiz.explain: Viewpoint shapes appearance, not all underlying facts.

quiz.prompt: A photo lacks a reliable date. What should a report do?
choices: State uncertainty or verify the date
Use upload time as event time
quiz.answer: State uncertainty or verify the date
quiz.explain: Publication time and capture time may differ.

quiz.prompt: Which edit most threatens documentary meaning?
quiz.explain: Removing substantive content can misrepresent the scene.

quiz.prompt: Why compare a crop with the wider image?
choices: Inspect context omitted by the crop
quiz.answer: Inspect context omitted by the crop
quiz.explain: The wider view can reveal what selection omitted.

quiz.prompt: A diagram can be valuable because it?
quiz.explain: Diagrams help explain relationships but remain models.

quiz.prompt: A close crop shows a crowded corner of an otherwise empty hall. Write guidance for an honest caption and image selection.
quiz.answer: Preserve relevant context by showing or explaining the wider view. The caption should describe the visible crowd without claiming the whole hall was full, and disclose meaningful cropping when it affects interpretation.
quiz.explain: Preserve relevant context by showing or explaining the wider view. The caption should describe the visible crowd without claiming the whole hall was full, and disclose meaningful cropping when it affects interpretation.

nodes.title: Reporting, Interviews and Editorial Judgement
nodes.goal: Produce a sourced report that separates observation, attribution and interpretation.
learning_outcomes: Match claims with appropriate sources.
Distinguish attribution from verification.
Apply evidence-sensitive editorial judgement.

lesson.overview: Reporting turns questions into a documented account through observation, records and interviews. Sources differ in what they know, what they have directly observed and what interests they hold. Fair reporting gives relevant claims a chance to be examined without treating unsupported assertions as equal to strong evidence. Attribution tells readers where information came from; verification asks whether it is accurate. Editorial judgement also weighs public relevance, privacy and the possibility that a vivid anecdote is unrepresentative.
lesson.worked_example: A report about a delayed bus route includes passenger accounts, a timetable and operator records. A passenger can describe their experience, while a frequency claim needs records across multiple days. The story separates the passenger’s account from the measured pattern.
lesson.activity: Write a fictional 400-word report from an evidence packet. Include a clear lead, attributed accounts, a checked numerical claim, a response to criticism and a note about unresolved facts.
lesson.reflection: Which compelling detail would you leave out because it is unsupported or needlessly intrusive?

quiz.prompt: Attribution tells the reader?
quiz.explain: Naming a source identifies provenance, not automatic accuracy.

quiz.prompt: One passenger’s bad trip establishes?
quiz.explain: Anecdotes do not by themselves estimate population patterns.

quiz.prompt: A useful interview question is?
choices: You agree with my claim, right?
quiz.explain: Open questions can separate observation from inference.

quiz.prompt: A numerical trend is best supported by?
choices: Relevant records and a clear method
quiz.answer: Relevant records and a clear method
quiz.explain: Systematic evidence is needed for claims about patterns.

quiz.prompt: Fair reporting requires unsupported claims to receive equal weight with strong evidence?
quiz.explain: Fairness includes evaluating evidence, not mechanical equivalence.

quiz.prompt: A source has a financial interest in a claim. The reporter should?
choices: Accept the account because of expertise
Disclose the interest and check claims
Reject the account because of interest
quiz.answer: Disclose the interest and check claims
quiz.explain: Interests matter but do not settle the truth of a claim.

quiz.prompt: A response opportunity helps?
choices: Replace the need for documentary checks
quiz.explain: A response can add context and reveal disputed facts.

quiz.prompt: An anonymous quote raises a need to?
choices: Publish private details to add credibility
quiz.explain: Anonymity requires careful editorial justification and corroboration.

quiz.prompt: Which lead is most defensible?
choices: The claim contradicted by the records
quiz.explain: A lead should reflect what the evidence establishes.

quiz.prompt: A correction should identify?
choices: A silent replacement of disputed wording
quiz.explain: Clear corrections support accountability and reader understanding.

quiz.prompt: A reporter has one passenger’s complaint and wants to claim an entire bus route is usually late. What additional work is needed?
quiz.answer: Attribute the passenger’s experience accurately, but verify the broader frequency claim using relevant records and a clear sampling period. Seek an operator response and report uncertainty or missing data.
quiz.explain: Attribute the passenger’s experience accurately, but verify the broader frequency claim using relevant records and a clear sampling period. Seek an operator response and report uncertainty or missing data.

nodes.title: Digital Platforms, Algorithms and Attention
nodes.goal: Analyze how ranking, incentives and data shape media exposure.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish ranking objectives from information quality.
Identify feedback between user behaviour and recommendations.
Evaluate attention metrics and their limits.

lesson.overview: A platform chooses what to display through a combination of rules, ranking systems and user choices. A recommender estimates outcomes such as relevance or likely engagement using available signals; it does not simply reveal what is objectively most important. Metrics create incentives for creators and platforms, and those incentives can favour attention-grabbing content. Exposure is also shaped by social networks, access and moderation. Analyzing a feed means distinguishing the platform’s objective, its data, the ranking process and the possible consequences.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional feed ranks posts by predicted viewing time. A sensational clip holds attention but contains little useful information. High ranking reflects the chosen objective and available signals, not proof that the clip is accurate or socially valuable.
lesson.activity: Rank six fictional posts using two objectives: likely viewing time and usefulness for a school project. Compare the resulting feeds and identify a trade-off and a missing signal.
lesson.reflection: What would your platform measure if its goal were informed understanding rather than time spent?

quiz.prompt: A highly ranked post is necessarily?
quiz.explain: Ranking reflects an objective and signals, not guaranteed truth.

quiz.prompt: A system optimizing viewing time may favour?
quiz.explain: Engagement and accuracy can differ.

quiz.prompt: A feedback loop occurs when?
choices: Behaviour has no role in ranking
quiz.explain: System outputs can influence the signals used for later outputs.

quiz.prompt: A click is an imperfect measure of interest because?
quiz.explain: The same observable action can have different meanings.

quiz.prompt: Moderation rules affect?
quiz.explain: Governance shapes availability but does not establish universal accuracy.

quiz.prompt: Comparing feeds from two accounts can show?
choices: The experience of the whole user base
quiz.explain: A small comparison provides bounded observations.

quiz.prompt: A platform objective should be evaluated alongside?
choices: The visual identity of the platform
quiz.explain: Optimization can produce trade-offs and side effects.

quiz.prompt: Why might a popularity signal disadvantage new creators?
choices: No potential for an interested audience
quiz.explain: Historical signals can privilege established visibility.

quiz.prompt: A recommendation explanation should ideally state?
choices: A claim that ranking involves no choices
Signals or criteria that influenced it
A claim to know the user’s intentions
quiz.answer: Signals or criteria that influenced it
quiz.explain: Transparency can help users understand the basis of ranking.

quiz.prompt: Improving a metric proves the underlying social goal improved?
choices: Not necessarily; it may be a proxy
Yes; a metric equals the social goal
quiz.answer: Not necessarily; it may be a proxy
quiz.explain: Metrics can be incomplete proxies for broader goals.

quiz.prompt: A feed ranks sensational posts highly because they attract long viewing times. Explain what the ranking does and does not establish.
quiz.answer: The objective rewards attention as measured by viewing time. That metric does not establish accuracy or understanding, and a feedback loop may amplify content that elicits the measured behaviour.
quiz.explain: The objective rewards attention as measured by viewing time. That metric does not establish accuracy or understanding, and a feedback loop may amplify content that elicits the measured behaviour.

nodes.title: Communication Theory and Media Institutions
nodes.goal: Compare theories of communication and connect them to testable questions.
learning_outcomes: Distinguish transmission, framing and agenda-setting questions.
Operationalize a theoretical concept.
Connect institutional conditions with media production.

lesson.overview: Communication theories highlight different parts of a complex process. Transmission models emphasize sender, message, channel and noise; interpretive approaches examine how people construct meaning in social contexts. Agenda-setting research asks how prominence in media relates to what audiences consider important, while framing examines how presentation organizes an issue. These concepts generate distinct questions and should not be collapsed into the claim that media simply control minds. Institutional analysis adds ownership, professional routines, regulation and resource constraints to explain how messages are produced.
lesson.worked_example: Two news outlets both cover housing often, but one emphasizes affordability and the other property investment. Their shared prominence relates to agenda-setting questions, while their different organizing perspectives invite framing analysis.
lesson.activity: Choose a fictional issue and develop two research questions using different theories. Define the concepts, propose observations and explain how institutional conditions could produce the messages.
lesson.reflection: What does your preferred theory make visible, and what does it leave in the background?

quiz.prompt: Agenda-setting research commonly examines?
quiz.explain: It studies attention to issues, not a blanket mind-control claim.

quiz.prompt: Framing concerns?
choices: The physical dimensions of a camera
The total size of the audience alone
quiz.explain: Frames foreground particular definitions, causes or evaluations.

quiz.prompt: A call is distorted so the listener misses words. What does the model need to account for?
choices: The length of the receiver’s name
The income of the message sender
quiz.explain: Noise can include disruptions that affect reception.

quiz.prompt: An interpretive approach emphasizes?
quiz.explain: Audiences interpret messages using social and cultural resources.

quiz.prompt: A theory becomes empirically useful when it?
quiz.explain: Testable implications let evidence bear on the explanation.

quiz.prompt: Ownership may influence media through?
quiz.explain: The influence must be analyzed through mechanisms, not assumed as uniform.

quiz.prompt: Two outlets cover an issue equally often but frame it differently. This distinguishes?
choices: Truth from falsehood in each account
quiz.explain: Frequency and organizing perspective are separate dimensions.

quiz.prompt: A correlation between coverage and concern establishes?
quiz.explain: Audience concern can also influence coverage or share external causes.

quiz.prompt: Operationalizing “prominence” might involve?
choices: The number of uses of the word media
quiz.explain: A construct needs transparent indicators.

quiz.prompt: Comparing theories is strongest when it?
quiz.explain: Theories are assessed by what they explain and how.

quiz.prompt: Two outlets cover housing equally often but one stresses affordability and the other investment. Formulate two distinct theoretical questions.
quiz.answer: An agenda-setting question asks whether prominence relates to audience importance. A framing question asks how the different perspectives shape interpretation, while recognizing that association alone does not establish causation.
quiz.explain: An agenda-setting question asks whether prominence relates to audience importance. A framing question asks how the different perspectives shape interpretation, while recognizing that association alone does not establish causation.

nodes.title: Media Research, Coding and Audience Evidence
nodes.goal: Design a content or audience study with transparent sampling and measurement.
learning_outcomes: Define a sampling frame and coding unit.
Distinguish coding reliability from validity.
Match content and audience methods to claims.

lesson.overview: Content analysis uses explicit categories to examine messages systematically. Researchers define a population, sampling frame, unit of analysis and codebook before drawing conclusions. Agreement between coders helps assess consistent application, but does not establish that the categories capture the intended meaning. Audience research adds surveys, interviews, experiments or observation to investigate reception and use. The method must match the claim: the presence of a message does not show that an audience encountered, understood or accepted it.
lesson.worked_example: A study codes 100 fictional news stories for whether they mention housing costs. Clear coding rules distinguish a passing mention from a central focus. A second coder checks a subset, while an audience survey separately asks what readers noticed.
lesson.activity: Create a codebook for ten supplied fictional messages. Define the unit and categories, independently code with a partner, discuss disagreements and revise the codebook before interpreting patterns.
lesson.reflection: Which audience claim would be unsupported by content data alone?

quiz.prompt: The unit of analysis could be?
choices: A defined post, story or sentence
A unit changed during each count
quiz.answer: A defined post, story or sentence
quiz.explain: A stable unit makes coding and comparison interpretable.

quiz.prompt: A codebook specifies?
quiz.explain: Explicit rules support transparent analysis.

quiz.prompt: High coder agreement proves the categories measure the right concept?
choices: Yes, a high score settles interpretation
quiz.explain: Consistency and construct validity are distinct.

quiz.prompt: A sample of trending posts represents all posts automatically?
choices: No, trending is a selected subset
quiz.answer: No, trending is a selected subset
quiz.explain: Trending selection excludes much of the population.

quiz.prompt: Finding a message in content proves an audience believed it?
quiz.explain: Exposure, understanding and belief require separate evidence.

quiz.prompt: A pilot coding exercise helps?
choices: Remove the need for inclusion criteria
Find ambiguous rules before full coding
quiz.answer: Find ambiguous rules before full coding
quiz.explain: Pilots can improve operational definitions.

quiz.prompt: Survey wording can influence answers through?
quiz.explain: Measurement depends partly on wording and response options.

quiz.prompt: Interviews with ten viewers most directly support?
quiz.explain: Qualitative depth does not automatically establish prevalence.

quiz.prompt: A sampling frame is?
choices: The result preferred by the hypothesis
The decorative border of the chart
quiz.explain: Coverage of the frame affects representativeness.

quiz.prompt: Reporting missing or uncodable data matters because?
quiz.explain: Readers need to assess potential selection and measurement problems.

quiz.prompt: Two coders agree on whether posts contain a slogan. A researcher concludes readers were persuaded. Explain the inference gap.
quiz.answer: Coder agreement supports reliability of the content coding, not an audience effect. Persuasion requires audience evidence about exposure and outcomes, plus an appropriate causal design for attribution.
quiz.explain: Coder agreement supports reliability of the content coding, not an audience effect. Persuasion requires audience evidence about exposure and outcomes, plus an appropriate causal design for attribution.

nodes.title: Graduate Media Effects and Causal Research
nodes.goal: Design and critique a causal study of media exposure with ethical and measurement limits.
learning_outcomes: Define exposure and outcome measures separately.
Distinguish assignment effects from treatment-received effects.
Critique identification, ethics and generalization.

lesson.overview: Media-effects research distinguishes exposure, attention, interpretation and outcomes rather than treating them as one variable. Randomized exposure can identify an intervention effect under a defined design, but artificial stimuli, noncompliance and spillovers may limit interpretation. Observational platform data often reflect selection because people choose content and systems respond to behaviour. Graduate work specifies an estimand, causal structure, measurement strategy and ethical safeguards before analysis. It evaluates whether a finding transfers across platforms, audiences and time, and separates statistical significance from practical importance.
lesson.worked_example: Volunteers are randomly assigned to two fictional headline styles. Some never read the assigned headline. An intention-to-treat analysis estimates the effect of assignment, not the effect of actually reading, and the study’s volunteer setting limits generalization.
lesson.activity: Write a preregistered protocol for a low-risk fictional media experiment. Define treatment, estimand, primary outcome, compliance measure, uncertainty analysis and debriefing. Add a causal diagram and critique both internal and external validity.
lesson.reflection: What would change if your intervention were delivered in an ordinary feed rather than a study session?

quiz.prompt: Intention-to-treat estimates the effect of?
quiz.explain: It compares groups as assigned even when compliance differs.

quiz.prompt: Users choose content that fits prior beliefs. This creates?
quiz.explain: Prior beliefs can influence both exposure and outcomes.

quiz.prompt: A statistically significant tiny effect may be?
quiz.explain: Significance and substantive magnitude are different.

quiz.prompt: A manipulation check measures?
choices: The full effect on each outcome
quiz.explain: It examines treatment implementation, with care about measurement effects.

quiz.prompt: Spillovers occur when?
quiz.explain: Interference can violate a simple individual-treatment model.

quiz.prompt: A preregistered primary outcome reduces?
quiz.explain: Advance specification constrains selective reporting.

quiz.prompt: A volunteer laboratory sample may limit?
choices: Transfer to ordinary users and settings
quiz.answer: Transfer to ordinary users and settings
quiz.explain: External validity concerns transfer beyond the study.

quiz.prompt: Controlling for a variable caused by treatment can?
choices: Alter or bias the intended estimate
quiz.answer: Alter or bias the intended estimate
quiz.explain: Post-treatment adjustment can block pathways or introduce bias.

quiz.prompt: A credible causal diagram should?
choices: Decorate the report with unexplained arrows
quiz.explain: The diagram makes assumptions explicit rather than proving them.

quiz.prompt: An ethical media study should minimize?
quiz.explain: Research design must consider participant welfare and informed participation.

quiz.prompt: Participants are assigned a headline but some never read it. Explain what an intention-to-treat estimate means and one limit.
quiz.answer: It estimates the effect of assignment, preserving the randomized comparison despite noncompliance. It does not directly identify the effect of actual reading, and generalization beyond the study population needs evidence.
quiz.explain: It estimates the effect of assignment, preserving the randomized comparison despite noncompliance. It does not directly identify the effect of actual reading, and generalization beyond the study population needs evidence.

nodes.title: Platform Governance and Communication Capstone
nodes.goal: Develop an evidence-based media governance or communication intervention with a critical evaluation plan.
learning_outcomes: Compare governance interventions using explicit objectives.
Analyze asymmetric errors and distributional effects.
Design accountable evaluation and revision mechanisms.

lesson.overview: Platform governance concerns how rules, ranking, moderation and appeals distribute opportunities and risks. A research-based intervention must define the problem carefully: reducing harmful reach, improving informed understanding and preserving participation are different goals. Measures can conflict, and effects may differ across languages and communities. A graduate capstone combines institutional analysis, stakeholder evidence and an evaluation design, then examines error costs and accountability. Transparent limitations and revision criteria matter especially when a proposed technical solution changes who can speak, be seen or challenge a decision.
lesson.worked_example: A fictional platform tests context labels on uncertain claims. Click-through falls, but some readers misunderstand the labels as a claim that every unlabelled post is true. The evaluation needs comprehension measures, subgroup analysis and a route to correct mistaken labels.
lesson.activity: Create a capstone proposal for a fictional platform or public-interest newsroom. Compare three interventions, define an error-cost matrix, plan mixed-method evaluation, document affected groups and specify review, appeal and revision procedures.
lesson.reflection: Which affected group might bear costs that your main success metric does not capture?

quiz.prompt: A false positive moderation decision means?
quiz.explain: The label is applied when the defined condition is absent.

quiz.prompt: A false negative means?
quiz.explain: The system fails to detect the condition it aims to identify.

quiz.prompt: Why analyze error costs separately?
quiz.explain: The distribution and severity of errors matter.

quiz.prompt: Lower sharing of a claim proves better understanding?
choices: Yes, a clear label proves understanding
quiz.explain: A behavioural metric is not a direct measure of comprehension.

quiz.prompt: An appeal mechanism supports?
quiz.explain: Contestability adds accountability when decisions can be wrong.

quiz.prompt: A multilingual rollout requires attention to?
quiz.explain: Language and context can change both errors and impacts.

quiz.prompt: A useful intervention comparison should share?
choices: A preference for the newest technology
quiz.explain: Common criteria make trade-offs assessable.

quiz.prompt: Stakeholder consultation alone establishes causal effectiveness?
choices: No, it informs goals and implementation
quiz.answer: No, it informs goals and implementation
quiz.explain: Participation evidence and causal evaluation answer different questions.

quiz.prompt: A revision threshold should specify?
choices: A commitment to preserve the first design
Evidence that triggers review or change
The date chosen for the public launch
quiz.answer: Evidence that triggers review or change
quiz.explain: Advance criteria make ongoing governance more accountable.

quiz.prompt: A strong capstone conclusion is?
quiz.explain: Graduate work connects evidence, values and limits.

quiz.prompt: A moderation pilot improves overall accuracy but wrongly removes more posts in a small language community. Propose an evaluation and governance response.
quiz.answer: Examine error distribution and severity by language, including false positives. Consult affected users, provide an appeal route and set revision criteria before expanding the pilot.
quiz.explain: Examine error distribution and severity by language, including false positives. Consult affected users, provide an appeal route and set revision criteria before expanding the pilot.
